Charcoal can absolutely hold a steady temperature for hours—if you treat it like a small furnace rather than a campfire. First, light the coals in two zones: pile two-thirds on one side of the grate and leave the other third empty. This creates the “hot side” for searing and the “cool side” for gentle holding. Once the coals are ash-gray (about 20 minutes), open the bottom vent halfway and the top vent a sliver—this gives you roughly 250 °F, perfect for slow cooking.

Add an extra 15 briquettes every 45 minutes to the hot zone; this maintains the heat without causing flare-ups. To keep burgers and dogs from drying out, move them to the cool zone once they’re wrapped in foil. Foil traps steam and keeps meat at a safe above-140 °F while you cook the next batch.

Pro tip: if the coals look too hot, close the top vent until it’s almost shut; if too cool, open both vents more. Think of it like adjusting the gas knob on a stove—just slower. I’ve kept brisket going for six hours this way and never had to babysit.
